proposedchanges.title: Trump Pardons Lynn Wade Barney for Firearm-Possession Conviction
proposedchanges.description_long: President Donald Trump pardoned Lynn Wade Barney on January 13, 2021, for a federal conviction in the District of Utah. The Justice Department lists the offense as possessing a firearm and ammunition after a prior felony conviction. Barney received 35 months in prison and three years of supervised release after the firearm-possession case. The prior felony meant federal law barred him from possessing a firearm. The public clemency listing does not describe the particular firearm or circumstances of possession. A presidential pardon forgives the federal conviction but does not erase the history of the case. Barney's pardon was part of the clemency actions Trump issued on his last day in office. The list confirms the date, offense and sentence, but does not state why Barney was selected for clemency. The pardon records federal relief from this conviction without resolving the underlying event or the administration's rationale.

evidencebasis: The latest medium and long identify Barney's 2021 pardon, firearm-possession offense, prior felony, District of Utah sentence, and absence of a stated rationale. The current metadata labels the pardon corrupt without evidence of an improper decision.
notes: The three source URLs remain intact. The proposed long keeps the listed facts and removes repeated source-audit commentary.

proposedchanges.title: Report Estimates $1.7 Million for Post-Presidency Secret Service Protection
proposedchanges.description_short: A report estimated $1.7 million in Secret Service costs for Trump family members and former officials during six months after he left office.
proposedchanges.description_long: After Donald Trump left office in January 2021, his adult children, their spouses and several former officials received Secret Service protection that cost about $1.7 million over six months, according to a Truthout report. It reported that former Treasury Secretary Steven Mnuchin's protection during travel to Israel and Qatar cost $52,000. The report also raised questions about payments to Trump properties when agents protected family members. Those payments created a potential conflict because Trump's businesses received government spending, but the supplied figures do not prove that every payment was improper or that Trump ordered coverage to benefit his properties. The report described the expanded protection as extraordinary, but the security basis for each person is not established in the available account. The figures document the reported cost and examples of coverage while leaving the reasons for individual protection decisions unclear.

evidencebasis: The latest medium identifies the six-month $1.7 million estimate, Mnuchin's $52,000 travel protection, and questions about payments to Trump properties. It explicitly says the evidence shows a potential conflict, not proof that every payment was improper.
notes: The Truthout URL remains intact. The proposed title, short, and long attribute the reported figures and remove the unsupported “scam” and “grift” framing.
